title: Does a sugar tax actually work?

turns.speaker: Lily
turns.text: The five-year figures are out. Sugar in soft drinks down about a third, and most of it happened before the tax even started.

turns.speaker: Lily
turns.text: It was announced two years ahead. The manufacturers reformulated to get under the threshold rather than pay it.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: So the tax barely collected anything, which everyone reported as a failure at the time.

turns.speaker: Andre
turns.text: That's genuinely clever policy design, then. You wanted the behaviour, not the money.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: The part I'd question is whether it moved anything that matters. Less sugar in one category isn't less sugar.

turns.speaker: Lily
turns.text: Total household sugar did fall. Not by as much as the drinks did, which suggests some of it came back as something else.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: And it's regressive, which the objectors were right about. Poorer households spend a larger share on the taxed thing.

turns.speaker: Lily
turns.text: They also carry more of the disease it causes, though, so they gain more from it working.

turns.speaker: Lily
turns.text: You can't call a policy regressive on the cost side and ignore who collects the benefit.

turns.speaker: Andre
turns.text: That's fair. Although that argument would justify a lot of things people would hate.

turns.speaker: Ruth
turns.text: It would. Which is why I'd keep it to the cases where reformulation is actually possible.

points: Five years on, sugar in soft drinks fell by about a third, mostly before the tax took effect.
The two-year notice led manufacturers to reformulate below the threshold rather than pay, so little revenue was collected.
Andre reads that as good design, since the aim was the behaviour rather than the money.
Total household sugar fell less than drink sugar, suggesting partial substitution into other products.
Ruth accepts the regressive criticism, that poorer households spend a larger share on the taxed item.
Lily answers that those households also carry more of the related disease, so they gain more when it works; Ruth would limit such taxes to cases where reformulation is possible.
